stem: In which class of airspace can a Part 107 pilot operate without prior authorization?

choices.text: Class G
Class B
Class D

explanation.correct: Class G (uncontrolled) airspace does not require prior authorization.
explanation.reason: Class G is uncontrolled airspace, so 14 CFR 107.41 does not apply to it. Class B and Class D are controlled airspace, and 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization (LAANC or FAA DroneZone) before a small unmanned aircraft operates in them.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class G never needs airspace authorization. Class B, C, and D always do, and Class E needs it only inside the surface area designated for an airport.

stem: What type of airspace is designated by a 'P' followed by a number on a sectional chart?

choices.text: Private airport
Parachute jump area
Prohibited area

explanation.correct: A 'P' designation indicates a prohibited area.
explanation.reason: Prohibited areas (for example P-56 over the White House) are established for security or national welfare and are charted with a 'P' and a number. Private airports and parachute jump areas use different chart symbols.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Under 14 CFR 107.45 you may not fly in a prohibited or restricted area without permission from the using or controlling agency. In practice, plan to stay out of prohibited areas entirely.

stem: What system provides near-real-time airspace authorization for Part 107 operations in controlled airspace?

choices.text: NOTAM
LAANC
ATIS

explanation.correct: LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability) provides near-real-time authorization.
explanation.reason: LAANC, the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability, automates airspace authorization using UAS Facility Maps that set the highest altitude that can be approved in each grid. Approved apps request and receive authorization in near-real time. A NOTAM is a notice about a time-critical condition or restriction and grants nothing. ATIS is a recorded broadcast of weather and airport information at busier airports.
explanation.keyTakeaway: LAANC is the fastest way to get authorization. Where LAANC is not available, request authorization through FAA DroneZone well ahead of the flight.

stem: How is Class E airspace that extends to the surface depicted on a sectional chart?

choices.text: Dashed magenta line
Solid magenta shading
Solid blue circle

explanation.correct: A dashed magenta line indicates Class E airspace that extends to the surface.
explanation.reason: The dashed magenta line is critical for Part 107 pilots because it indicates where Class E begins at the surface (requiring authorization). A faded magenta shading indicates where Class E transitions from 1,200 AGL down to 700 AGL — still Class G at the surface.
explanation.keyTakeaway: DASHED magenta = Class E to surface = authorization required. FADED magenta shading = Class E starts at 700 AGL, so below 700 AGL is still Class G.

stem: What is indicated by a Military Training Route labeled 'IR-206' on a sectional chart?

choices.text: An IFR military training route with at least one segment above 1,500 feet AGL
A VFR military training route that is flown entirely at or below 1,500 feet AGL
Restricted airspace reserved for military operations

explanation.correct: IR means the route is flown under IFR, and a three-digit number means at least one segment is above 1,500 feet AGL.
explanation.reason: Military training routes are labeled IR (flown under IFR) or VR (flown under VFR). A three-digit number means one or more segments are above 1,500 feet AGL. A four-digit number means the whole route is at or below 1,500 feet AGL. An MTR is not restricted airspace, so no permission is needed, but military aircraft may be moving faster than 250 knots.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Four digits = entire route at or below 1,500 feet AGL, which is where drones fly. Three digits = at least one segment above 1,500 feet AGL.

stem: Which type of special-use airspace is NOT depicted on VFR sectional charts?

choices.text: Military Operations Areas (MOA)
Restricted Areas
Controlled Firing Areas (CFA)

explanation.correct: Controlled Firing Areas (CFA) are NOT depicted on VFR sectional charts.
explanation.reason: A controlled firing area holds activities that could be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft, but the activity is suspended as soon as spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookouts see an aircraft approaching. Because nonparticipating aircraft never have to change course, CFAs are not charted. MOAs and restricted areas are charted.
explanation.keyTakeaway: CFAs are 'invisible' on charts because they suspend operations when aircraft approach. All other special-use airspace is charted.

stem: Class B airspace surrounding major airports typically extends from the surface up to:

choices.text: 18,000 feet MSL
2,500 feet AGL
10,000 feet MSL

explanation.correct: Class B airspace typically extends from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL.
explanation.reason: Class B airspace surrounds the nation's busiest airports and generally extends from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL. Each Class B area is individually tailored and looks like an upside-down wedding cake. 18,000 feet MSL is the floor of Class A, and 2,500 feet AGL is the typical top of Class D.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class B = 'Big' airports (major commercial). Goes from surface to typically 10,000 MSL in an inverted wedding cake shape.

stem: During night operations under Part 107, what lighting is required on the sUAS?

choices.text: Navigation lights visible for at least 1 statute mile
No lighting is required if the pilot has completed night training
Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles

explanation.correct: Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles is required.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.29 requires lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles, with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision, during night and civil twilight operations. The remote PIC may reduce the intensity, but not turn the light off, if doing so is in the interest of safety. Night training does not replace the lighting requirement.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Night and civil twilight flights need anti-collision lighting visible for 3 statute miles. Statute miles, not nautical.

stem: A Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) is issued for a presidential visit. What should a Part 107 pilot do?

choices.text: Contact the local tower for clearance to fly
Request a waiver through LAANC
Check NOTAMs and avoid the TFR area completely

explanation.correct: Check NOTAMs and avoid the TFR area completely.
explanation.reason: VIP temporary flight restrictions are issued by FDC NOTAM under 14 CFR 91.141, and 14 CFR 107.47 requires remote pilots to comply with them. A control tower cannot clear a drone into the TFR, and LAANC grants controlled-airspace authorization, not relief from a TFR.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Check for TFRs before every flight. A LAANC authorization does not override a TFR.

stem: On a sectional chart, a job site lies inside a solid blue ring labeled 100 over 40 (100/40). The ground there is at 600 feet MSL, and no other airspace is charted beneath the ring. A drone flown at 300 feet AGL at this site is:

choices.text: Inside Class B airspace, so ATC authorization is required before the flight
Below the floor of Class B airspace, so no ATC authorization is needed
Inside Class A airspace

explanation.correct: Below the floor of Class B airspace, so no ATC authorization is needed.
explanation.reason: Solid blue lines mark Class B airspace, and the numbers give its ceiling and floor in hundreds of feet MSL. 100/40 means Class B from 4,000 to 10,000 feet MSL in that ring. A drone at 300 feet AGL over 600-foot terrain is at 900 feet MSL, far below the 4,000-foot floor. Class A begins at 18,000 feet MSL.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Read the Class B fraction: top number is the ceiling, bottom number is the floor, both in hundreds of feet MSL. SFC means it reaches the ground.

stem: How is Class B airspace depicted on a sectional chart?

choices.text: Solid magenta lines
Dashed blue lines
Solid blue lines

explanation.correct: Solid blue lines.
explanation.reason: Class B airspace is outlined with solid blue lines. Solid magenta lines outline Class C, and dashed blue lines outline Class D.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Solid blue = B. Solid magenta = C. Dashed blue = D. Dashed magenta = Class E at the surface.

stem: A remote pilot plans to fly at 200 feet AGL beneath the outer shelf of Class C airspace. The shelf is labeled 43 over 15 (43/15), field elevation is 300 feet MSL, and the airspace below the shelf is Class G. Is ATC authorization required?

choices.text: Yes, because any flight inside the outer ring of Class C needs authorization
No, because the drone stays below the 1,500-foot MSL floor of the shelf
Yes, because Class C always extends to the surface

explanation.correct: No, because the drone stays below the 1,500-foot MSL floor of the shelf.
explanation.reason: The label 43/15 means the Class C shelf extends from 1,500 feet MSL to 4,300 feet MSL. A drone at 200 feet AGL over 300-foot terrain is at 500 feet MSL, below the shelf and in Class G airspace. Only the inner core of Class C, labeled with SFC, extends to the surface.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class C has an inner surface area and an outer shelf. Under the shelf you are not in Class C.

stem: Which description fits the usual shape of Class C airspace?

choices.text: A single 4 NM radius cylinder from the surface up to 2,500 feet above the airport, with no shelf areas
A 5 NM radius core from the surface and a 10 NM radius shelf from 1,200 feet, both up to 4,000 feet above the airport
A 30 NM radius area from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, with several layered shelves

explanation.correct: A 5 NM radius core from the surface and a 10 NM radius shelf from 1,200 feet, both up to 4,000 feet above the airport.
explanation.reason: The AIM describes Class C airspace as usually having a 5 NM radius surface area that extends to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation, and a 10 NM radius shelf area from 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation. A single small cylinder to 2,500 feet describes typical Class D. Each area is individually tailored.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class C: 5 NM core to the surface, 10 NM shelf starting at 1,200 feet above the airport.

stem: An airport is surrounded by a dashed blue line, and a dashed blue box nearby contains the number 27. What does the number mean?

choices.text: Class D extends from the surface up to and including 2,700 feet AGL
Class D extends from the surface up to and including 2,700 feet MSL
Class D begins at 2,700 feet MSL and extends upward to the base of Class A

explanation.correct: Class D extends from the surface up to and including 2,700 feet MSL.
explanation.reason: A dashed blue line marks Class D airspace. The number in the dashed box is the ceiling of the Class D airspace in hundreds of feet MSL, so 27 means 2,700 feet MSL. A minus sign in front of the number would mean up to but not including that altitude.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class D ceiling: number in the dashed box, hundreds of feet MSL.

stem: A Class D airport has a part-time control tower. A remote pilot wants to fly 1 mile from the airport after the tower has closed for the night. What should the pilot do first?

choices.text: Fly without checking further, because all airspace becomes Class G whenever a control tower is closed
Phone the closed tower and leave a message describing the flight
Check the Chart Supplement to see what class of airspace is in effect when the tower is closed

explanation.correct: Check the Chart Supplement to see what class of airspace is in effect when the tower is closed.
explanation.reason: When a part-time tower closes, the Class D airspace changes to either Class E surface area or Class G, as published in the Chart Supplement. If it becomes a Class E surface area designated for the airport, 14 CFR 107.41 still requires authorization. If it becomes Class G, it does not. A voicemail is not an authorization.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Tower closed does not always mean Class G. The Chart Supplement tells you what the airspace becomes.

stem: A small non-towered airport sits inside an area of shaded (fading) magenta on the sectional chart. No dashed lines surround the airport. At what altitude does Class E airspace begin there?

choices.text: The surface
700 feet AGL
1,200 feet AGL

explanation.correct: 700 feet AGL.
explanation.reason: Shaded magenta marks areas where the floor of Class E airspace is 700 feet AGL. Below that, down to the surface, the airspace is Class G. Class E at the surface would be shown by a dashed magenta line. A 1,200-foot AGL floor is what applies in most areas outside the magenta shading.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Fuzzy magenta = Class E starts at 700 feet AGL, so a drone at or below 400 feet AGL there is in Class G.

stem: A dashed magenta line encloses a rectangular Class E extension that juts out from a Class D airport's dashed blue circle. A remote pilot plans to fly at 200 feet AGL inside the extension, outside the Class D circle. Is ATC authorization required?

choices.text: Yes. All airspace enclosed by a dashed magenta line requires ATC authorization at any altitude
Yes. Class E airspace always requires ATC authorization for any flight that is conducted below 400 feet AGL
No. Authorization is needed only in the Class E surface area designated for an airport, not in an extension

explanation.correct: No. Authorization is needed only in the Class E surface area designated for an airport, not in an extension.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires authorization in Class B, C, or D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport. FAA guidance treats Class E surface extensions to Class B, C, or D airspace as not covered by that rule. The pilot must still stay out of the Class D circle and avoid interfering with airport traffic.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class E surface area for an airport: authorization. Class E extension: no authorization, but stay alert for arriving and departing aircraft.

stem: A remote pilot is flying at 350 feet AGL, 3 miles from a non-towered airport that is depicted in magenta with shaded magenta around it. In what class of airspace is the drone?

choices.text: Class E
Class D
Class G

explanation.correct: Class G.
explanation.reason: Shaded magenta means Class E begins at 700 feet AGL, so from the surface to 700 feet AGL the airspace is Class G. Class D would be shown with a dashed blue line and needs an operating control tower. Being near an airport does not by itself make the airspace controlled.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Most low-altitude drone flying happens in Class G. The chart, not the presence of an airport, tells you the class.

stem: A planned flight is inside an active military operations area (MOA). What does Part 107 require?

choices.text: No permission is required, but the pilot should use extra caution
Permission from the using agency is required, as for a restricted area
A LAANC authorization is required whenever the MOA is active

explanation.correct: No permission is required, but the pilot should use extra caution.
explanation.reason: A MOA separates certain military training from IFR traffic. Flight in a MOA is not prohibited, and 14 CFR 107.45 covers only prohibited and restricted areas. The AIM advises extreme caution when a MOA is active. LAANC applies to controlled airspace around airports.
explanation.keyTakeaway: MOA = caution, not permission. Check the chart or NOTAMs for its hours and altitudes.

stem: Which statement describes a warning area?

choices.text: Airspace from 3 NM outward from the U.S. coast that may contain hazardous activity
Airspace over a national park where flight below 2,000 feet AGL should be avoided
Airspace around a towered airport where two-way radio contact is required

explanation.correct: Airspace from 3 NM outward from the U.S. coast that may contain hazardous activity.
explanation.reason: The AIM defines a warning area as airspace of defined dimensions, extending from 3 nautical miles outward from the coast of the United States, that contains activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft. It may lie over domestic or international waters.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Warning area = offshore hazard area, charted with a W and a number.

stem: What does an alert area (for example A-211) on a sectional chart tell a remote pilot?

choices.text: Flight within the area is prohibited at all times without permission
It may contain a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity
A temporary flight restriction is in effect there until further notice

explanation.correct: It may contain a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity.
explanation.reason: Alert areas are charted to inform pilots of areas that may contain a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity. No permission is needed, and everyone flying there remains responsible for collision avoidance. Prohibited areas are marked with a P, and temporary flight restrictions are issued by NOTAM.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Alert area: legal to fly, but expect a lot of traffic.

stem: A sectional chart shows a gray line labeled VR1207 crossing a planned drone flight area. What should the remote pilot expect?

choices.text: Military aircraft under VFR at or below 1,500 feet AGL, possibly above 250 knots
Military aircraft under IFR, always above 1,500 feet AGL and below 250 knots
A restricted area that requires permission from the using agency to enter

explanation.correct: Military aircraft under VFR at or below 1,500 feet AGL, possibly above 250 knots.
explanation.reason: VR marks a military training route flown under VFR. A four-digit number means no segment of the route is above 1,500 feet AGL. Aircraft on these routes may exceed 250 knots. A military training route is not restricted airspace, and no permission is needed, but the route is flown at the altitudes drones use.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Four-digit route = low route. Treat it as a strong reason to use a visual observer and keep listening and looking.

stem: A sectional chart shows a national security area (NSA) over an industrial site. What is a remote pilot expected to do?

choices.text: Voluntarily avoid flying through the area, and check NOTAMs in case flight has been prohibited
Nothing at all, because a national security area is only a chart label and carries no request or restriction
Request a LAANC authorization before entering

explanation.correct: Voluntarily avoid flying through the area, and check NOTAMs in case flight has been prohibited.
explanation.reason: The AIM describes national security areas as airspace where pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying, because of a need for increased security and safety of ground facilities. Flight can be temporarily prohibited by NOTAM under 14 CFR 99.7, and 14 CFR 107.47 then requires compliance.
explanation.keyTakeaway: National security area: avoidance is requested, and it becomes mandatory when a NOTAM says so.

stem: A job site lies within a terminal radar service area (TRSA), outside the Class D airspace of the primary airport, in Class G airspace at the surface. What authorization does the remote pilot need for a flight at 300 feet AGL?

choices.text: A LAANC authorization, because a TRSA is controlled in the same way as Class C
None, because a TRSA is not a class of airspace that requires authorization
Permission from the using agency that operates the radar service

explanation.correct: None, because a TRSA is not a class of airspace that requires authorization.
explanation.reason: A TRSA is an area where participating pilots can receive additional radar services. It does not fit any of the airspace classes and is not regulatory. 14 CFR 107.41 requires authorization only in Class B, C, D, and the surface area of Class E designated for an airport, so the primary airport's Class D still needs authorization, but the Class G site does not.
explanation.keyTakeaway: TRSA rings (solid black or gray) do not change the airspace class. Look at what class actually lies under them.

stem: A remote pilot is working in Class G airspace during the day. Scattered cloud bases are at 800 feet AGL and visibility is 5 statute miles. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The drone only has to remain clear of clouds, because the airspace is Class G
The drone may fly up to 400 feet AGL, because the visibility is above 3 statute miles
The drone must stay at or below 300 feet AGL and 2,000 feet horizontally from the clouds

explanation.correct: The drone must stay at or below 300 feet AGL and 2,000 feet horizontally from the clouds.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.51 sets the same minimums in every class of airspace: 3 statute miles visibility, 500 feet below clouds, and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. 800 - 500 = 300 feet AGL. 'Clear of clouds' is a Part 91 rule for manned aircraft in some Class G airspace and does not apply to Part 107.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part 107 weather minimums do not change with airspace class. Do not borrow the manned-aircraft VFR table.

stem: A LAANC app shows a UAS Facility Map grid value of 100 over a job site in Class C airspace. What does this mean?

choices.text: Requests at or below 100 feet AGL can be authorized in near-real time
Drones must stay at least 100 feet away from all people and structures
Flight is prohibited below 100 feet AGL anywhere inside that grid square

explanation.correct: Requests at or below 100 feet AGL can be authorized in near-real time.
explanation.reason: UAS Facility Maps show the maximum altitude, in feet AGL, at which the FAA can authorize Part 107 operations in each grid without additional safety analysis. A request at or below the grid value can be approved through LAANC in near-real time. Higher requests, up to 400 feet, need further coordination with ATC.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The grid value is a ceiling for automatic approval, measured in feet AGL.

stem: A remote pilot has a LAANC authorization for 200 feet AGL in Class D airspace. On arrival, visibility at the site is 2 statute miles in haze. May the flight be made?

choices.text: No, because the authorization does not change the 3-statute-mile visibility minimum
Yes, because an ATC authorization overrides the Part 107 weather minimums
Yes, provided the pilot stays below 100 feet AGL and uses a visual observer throughout

explanation.correct: No, because the authorization does not change the 3-statute-mile visibility minimum.
explanation.reason: An airspace authorization satisfies 14 CFR 107.41 only. Every other Part 107 rule still applies, including the 3-statute-mile visibility minimum in 14 CFR 107.51. Relief from the visibility rule would need a certificate of waiver.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Authorization gets you into the airspace. It does not relax any other rule.

stem: A remote pilot plans to fly a quarter mile from the runway of a non-towered airport in Class G airspace. Under Part 107, the pilot:

choices.text: Must notify the airport manager at least 24 hours before the flight takes place
Must stay at least 5 miles from the airport unless the airport operator approves the flight
Needs no authorization, but must not interfere with airport operations or traffic patterns

explanation.correct: Needs no authorization, but must not interfere with airport operations or traffic patterns.
explanation.reason: Class G airspace needs no ATC authorization. 14 CFR 107.43 prohibits operating a small unmanned aircraft in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base, and 107.37 requires yielding to all aircraft. Part 107 has no 5-mile rule and no notification rule.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Near a Class G airport: legal without authorization, but manned traffic comes first. Monitor the CTAF and stay clear of the pattern.

stem: A remote pilot sees a large unmanned free balloon drifting toward the flight area. What does the AIM advise?

choices.text: Fly directly beneath it, where the air is calmer
Avoid flying beneath it
Climb to pass close to it for a better look

explanation.correct: Avoid flying beneath it.
explanation.reason: The AIM advises against flight beneath unmanned balloons. They often carry payloads and trailing lines or antennas that are hard to see, and a payload may be released or fall. Flying beneath one is exactly the hazard the AIM warns about, however calm the air there seems. Climbing close for a look brings the drone near those lines and the payload.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Never fly under an unmanned balloon.

stem: Why should a remote pilot avoid flying a drone over or close to an operating smoke stack or cooling tower?

choices.text: The structure blocks GPS reception for several miles in every direction
The rising plume can cause turbulence and loss of control, and may be invisible
Smoke stacks and cooling towers are always located inside restricted areas

explanation.correct: The rising plume can cause turbulence and loss of control, and may be invisible.
explanation.reason: The AIM warns that thermal plumes from smoke stacks and cooling towers can produce significant turbulence and can affect aircraft performance and control, and that a plume may be invisible. The hazard is strongest in calm wind and close to the stack.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Give smoke stacks and cooling towers a wide berth, staying upwind when you can.

stem: A remote pilot is inspecting farmland next to a tall guyed antenna tower. How far out from the tower can the supporting guy wires extend?

choices.text: No more than 100 feet horizontally
About 1,500 feet horizontally
Only as far as the tower's lights are visible

explanation.correct: About 1,500 feet horizontally.
explanation.reason: The AIM warns that guy wires can extend about 1,500 feet horizontally from a structure and are difficult to see, and it recommends avoiding skeletal structures by at least 2,000 feet horizontally. One hundred feet badly understates their reach. Lighting is no guide to where the wires are, because the lights are on the tower and the wires are not lighted.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Guy wires reach far beyond the tower and are close to invisible. Plan the flight path around them.

stem: Which is an acceptable way to get the current NOTAMs for a planned flight area?

choices.text: Call Flight Service at 1-800-WX-BRIEF or use the FAA's online NOTAM search
Read the notes printed on the most recent edition of the sectional chart
Listen to the nearest airport's ATIS broadcast and rely on that alone

explanation.correct: Call Flight Service at 1-800-WX-BRIEF or use the FAA's online NOTAM search.
explanation.reason: NOTAMs are time-critical notices that are not known far enough in advance to be published on charts. They are available from Flight Service, including by phone at 1-800-WX-BRIEF, and from the FAA's online NOTAM search. An ATIS broadcast may mention some local NOTAMs but is not a complete source.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Check NOTAMs before every flight. Charts cannot show temporary restrictions.

stem: Temporary flight restrictions are published in which type of NOTAM?

choices.text: FDC NOTAMs, which are regulatory
NOTAM (D), which only describes runway and taxiway conditions
Pointer NOTAMs, which are advisory only

explanation.correct: FDC NOTAMs, which are regulatory.
explanation.reason: Flight Data Center (FDC) NOTAMs carry regulatory information such as temporary flight restrictions and changes to instrument procedures. NOTAM (D) information covers conditions at airports and navigation facilities, such as runway closures and lighting outages, and is not where flight restrictions are issued. A pointer NOTAM only highlights another NOTAM so that it is not missed.
explanation.keyTakeaway: FDC NOTAM = regulatory. A TFR in an FDC NOTAM is binding on drone pilots.

stem: Which piece of personal equipment helps a remote pilot most with checklists and controller settings at night while protecting night vision?

choices.text: A bright white headlamp aimed at the controller
A flashlight with a dim red light
Polarized sunglasses

explanation.correct: A flashlight with a dim red light.
explanation.reason: The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains that dim red light has the least effect on dark adaptation, while white light degrades it quickly. Sunglasses reduce the light reaching the eyes and make night vision worse.
explanation.keyTakeaway: At night use the dimmest red light that lets you read. One blast of white light costs you many minutes of dark adaptation.

stem: At night a remote pilot sees a tower marked with steady and flashing red lights. During the day the same tower shows bright white strobes. These lights are:

choices.text: A signal that the tower is inside controlled airspace
Obstruction lighting that warns aircraft of the structure
A rotating beacon that marks a heliport

explanation.correct: Obstruction lighting that warns aircraft of the structure.
explanation.reason: The AIM describes obstruction lighting as aviation red obstruction lights at night, and medium- or high-intensity flashing white lights that may be used by day or night. The lighting marks the structure as a hazard and says nothing about the class of airspace. A heliport beacon flashes green, yellow, and white.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Red lights or white strobes on a structure mean an obstruction. Guy wires around it are not lighted.

stem: Why is a daylight survey of the site valuable before a night operation?

choices.text: Many obstacles, such as wires, trees, and shorter towers, are unlighted and cannot be seen at night
FAA rules require every obstacle to be lighted, so the survey is only needed to map where the lights are
Drones cannot record a home point in the dark

explanation.correct: Many obstacles, such as wires, trees, and shorter towers, are unlighted and cannot be seen at night.
explanation.reason: Obstruction lighting is generally required only on taller structures, so power lines, trees, and many structures below about 200 feet AGL have no lights. AC 107-2A recommends learning the location of ground hazards before night operations because they are hard to see in the dark.
explanation.keyTakeaway: If it is not lighted, you will not see it at night. Find the hazards in daylight.

stem: At night a remote pilot sees an airplane's red light and green light at the same time, with the red light on the observer's right. The airplane is:

choices.text: Flying away from the observer
Flying toward the observer
Crossing from right to left

explanation.correct: Flying toward the observer.
explanation.reason: An airplane carries a red position light on its left wingtip, a green light on its right wingtip, and a white light on its tail. Seeing red and green together means the observer is looking at the front of the airplane. With the airplane's left wing on the observer's right, it is head-on. Seen from behind, only the white tail light would show.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Red and green together = it is coming at you. Descend and get out of the way.

stem: A remote pilot asks for authorization to fly in Class C airspace and is refused. Which is a valid basis for ATC to deny the request?

choices.text: Traffic density or controller workload at the time
The drone lacks geofencing beyond what Part 107 requires
The remote pilot does not carry a two-way aviation radio

explanation.correct: Traffic density or controller workload at the time.
explanation.reason: AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10, says the FAA may approve or deny operations based on traffic density, controller workload, communication issues, or any other type of operation that could affect the safe and expeditious flow of air traffic. Paragraph 5.10.2 says the Air Traffic Organization does not approve or deny requests on the basis of equipage beyond the Part 107 requirements, such as geofencing. Part 107 does not require a radio, so its absence is not the basis for the decision.
explanation.keyTakeaway: ATC decides on traffic, workload, and safety of the flow, not on extra drone equipment.

stem: A remote pilot has ATC authorization to fly up to 400 feet AGL in Class B airspace. Flight visibility from the control station is 3 statute miles, and the ceiling is broken at 600 feet AGL. What is the highest the drone may fly?

choices.text: 400 feet AGL
100 feet AGL
No flight is allowed

explanation.correct: 100 feet AGL.
explanation.reason: Part 107 has a single set of weather minimums for every class of airspace. 14 CFR 107.51(c) requires 3 statute miles of flight visibility from the control station, which is met, and 107.51(d) requires staying at least 500 feet below clouds. With cloud bases at 600 feet AGL, the drone may fly no higher than 100 feet AGL. 400 feet AGL would apply only if the cloud base were 900 feet AGL or higher, which mixes up the manned-aircraft idea that Class B only requires staying clear of clouds. The flight is allowed, because the 3-statute-mile visibility minimum is met; Part 107 has no 5-mile requirement in Class B.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part 107 weather minimums are the same in every airspace: 3 SM visibility, 500 ft below and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.

stem: In Class G airspace, a remote pilot hovers a drone 200 feet above the end of a runway at a non-towered airport. An airplane holding short delays its takeoff until the drone leaves. No collision was ever likely. Did the pilot violate Part 107?

choices.text: No, because the drone did not violate the right-of-way rule
Yes, by interfering with operations at the airport
Yes, by flying in Class G airspace without an authorization

explanation.correct: Yes, by interfering with operations at the airport.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.43 prohibits operating in a manner that interferes with operations and traffic patterns at any airport. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10.1.1, describes this exact case: a drone hovering 200 feet above a runway causes an airplane holding short to delay takeoff. That interferes with airport operations even though it does not violate 107.37(a). Class G needs no authorization; the violation is the interference prohibited by 107.43.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Causing manned traffic to change its plans is interference, even with no collision risk.

stem: A remote pilot is behind schedule and skips the site survey and preflight checklist to get the job done. According to the AIM's list of the most frequent general aviation accident causal factors, this is an example of:

choices.text: Improper in-flight decisions or planning after takeoff
Inadequate preflight preparation and/or planning
Failure to see and avoid objects or obstructions

explanation.correct: Inadequate preflight preparation and/or planning.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-1 lists the 10 most frequent causal factors for general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command, and the first is inadequate preflight preparation and/or planning. Skipping the site survey and checklist before the flight is exactly that. Improper in-flight decisions and failure to see and avoid objects are also on the list, but they describe failures during the flight, not before it.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Rushed or skipped preflight planning is the first item on the AIM's accident list.

stem: A remote pilot hears on the CTAF that an airplane may have a landing gear problem and thinks about flying the drone close to it to take a look. What is correct?

choices.text: Fly up to it only if the airplane's pilot asks for help on the radio
Stay away; close flight near another aircraft is hazardous
Stay below it at 100 feet so its pilot can see the drone

explanation.correct: Stay away; close flight near another aircraft is hazardous.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-11 says close-proximity in-flight inspection of another aircraft is uniquely hazardous and that pilots receive little or no training for it. 14 CFR 107.37 requires the drone to yield the right of way to all aircraft and prohibits operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard. A request from the other pilot does not authorize this, and no fixed distance makes it safe. Holding position close below the airplane is still flying near another aircraft; 107.37(b) prohibits creating a collision hazard.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Airborne inspections are hazardous even for trained crews. A drone must stay well clear.

stem: What causes precipitation static (P-static), and what is one of its effects?

choices.text: Nearby lightning strikes; structural icing on the airframe
Static from the aircraft's battery; lithium thermal runaway
Charge from flying through particles; noisy or lost radio

explanation.correct: Charge from flying through particles; noisy or lost radio.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-12 says P-static is caused by an aircraft in flight coming into contact with uncharged particles such as rain, snow, fog, sleet, hail, volcanic ash, or dust, which builds a negative charge on the airframe. Reported effects include complete loss of VHF communications, erroneous compass readings, a high-pitched squeal on audio, and erratic instrument readings. It is not caused by lightning, does not cause icing, and has nothing to do with battery thermal runaway.
explanation.keyTakeaway: P-static: charge from flying through particles, heard as radio noise or lost communications.

stem: A remote pilot sees a laser beam illuminate a manned helicopter near the job site and hears the helicopter pilot report it. According to the AIM, how should pilots report laser illumination?

choices.text: To ATC or flight service as soon as possible after it happens
To the FAA within 10 days, the same as a Part 107 accident report
No report is needed unless someone on board is injured

explanation.correct: To ATC or flight service as soon as possible after it happens.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-13 says pilots should report laser illumination to the controlling ATC facility, Federal Contract Tower, or flight service station as soon as possible after the event, including the UTC date and time, call sign, aircraft type, nearest city, altitude, location, and a description. The 10-day report in 14 CFR 107.9 is for serious injury, loss of consciousness, or damage to property other than the drone where the repair cost or fair market value exceeds $500. The AIM does not limit laser reports to injury cases.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Lasers: report as soon as possible, with time, place, and altitude.

stem: Why does the AIM advise pilots to avoid flying beneath unmanned free balloons?

choices.text: Balloons are required to carry hazardous material for weather sensors
A payload below it is always lit and easy to see
A payload or trailing antenna below it may be nearly invisible

explanation.correct: A payload or trailing antenna below it may be nearly invisible.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-5 says most unmanned free balloons have a suspension device with a payload, a trailing wire antenna, or both, extending below them, and these may be invisible until an aircraft is close. For that reason, flight below them should be avoided at all times, and sightings should be reported to the nearest FAA ground facility. The AIM does not cite hazardous material as the reason. Payloads and suspension lines are not always lit or easy to see; that is the hazard.
explanation.keyTakeaway: What hangs below a balloon may be invisible. Never fly underneath.

stem: On a calm, cold morning, a remote pilot must inspect a structure next to an operating power plant stack. According to the AIM, what should the pilot expect from the exhaust plume?

choices.text: Its effects are worst in calm, cold air and may be invisible, so stay well clear
The plume is harmless whenever no smoke or steam can be seen
In calm air the plume rises straight up, so flying beside the stack is safe

explanation.correct: Its effects are worst in calm, cold air and may be invisible, so stay well clear.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-16 says exhaust plume effects are more pronounced in calm, stable air when the plume is very hot and the surrounding air is cold. It also says plumes can be invisible and stacks with no visible plume may still be operating, and that pilots should steer clear by flying on the upwind side when able. Some studies predict turbulent effects more than 1,000 feet above the top of the stack.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Calm and cold makes plumes worse. Visible or not, stay clear and upwind.

stem: A remote pilot is surveying low along a river canyon in a rural area. What does the AIM say about overhead wires in such areas?

choices.text: Lines often span rivers and canyons and may be nearly impossible to see
Wires crossing rivers are always marked with lighted spherical markers
All wires below 200 feet AGL are shown on sectional charts

explanation.correct: Lines often span rivers and canyons and may be nearly impossible to see.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-4 says overhead transmission and utility lines often span natural flyways such as lakes, rivers, gorges, and canyons, and the wires may be virtually impossible to see under certain conditions. Spherical markers may be used but are not always present. The AIM also warns that at and below 200 feet AGL many power lines and towers are not marked, lighted, or charted.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Rivers, canyons, and highways attract wires, and many are unmarked and uncharted.

stem: Which equipment plan for a night job follows the PHAK's guidance on personal lighting?

choices.text: One bright white flashlight, left on throughout the flight
No flashlight, because the controller screen gives enough light
Two flashlights, one of them small and dimmable

explanation.correct: Two flashlights, one of them small and dimmable.
explanation.reason: The PHAK (FAA-H-8083-25C, Chapter 2) recommends carrying at least two flashlights for night flight: one for the exterior preflight and a smaller one that can be dimmed and kept nearby. A bright white light used during the flight works against night vision adaptation (PHAK Chapter 17), and a controller screen does not light the equipment or the launch area.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Two lights at night: one for preflight, one small and dimmable for use during the flight.

stem: At night, a remote pilot sees two tall towers whose white strobes flash in sequence: middle, then top, then bottom. What do these lights indicate?

choices.text: The towers are part of an airport approach lighting system
The towers are under construction and have not yet been charted
Wires are strung between the structures and may be hard to see

explanation.correct: Wires are strung between the structures and may be hard to see.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-4 says some support structures for overhead transmission lines have unique sequence-flashing white strobe systems to show that there are wires between the structures, flashing in the order middle, top, bottom. It is not an approach lighting system, and the flash sequence says nothing about construction status.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Middle-top-bottom white strobes on towers mean wires between them.

stem: A remote pilot plans a night survey of a rural wind farm site. What hazard does the AIM highlight that may be hard to see?

choices.text: Short meteorological towers with guy wires
Wind turbines, because the FAA does not chart them
Nothing, because every structure at a wind farm is lighted at night

explanation.correct: Short meteorological towers with guy wires.
explanation.reason: AIM 7-6-4 says meteorological towers used by wind energy companies may be under 200 feet AGL, can be put up in a matter of hours, use guy wires, and are often hard to see, and that not all of them follow the marking guidelines. The same paragraph says that at and below 200 feet AGL there are numerous power lines and towers that are not marked and lighted, and that not all wind turbines in a farm need to be lighted. Wind turbines are typically charted on sectional charts.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Short meteorological towers with guy wires can go up overnight, unlit and unmarked.

stem: During a daytime job, a remote pilot notices a manned airplane flying with a flashing anti-collision beacon. What does this most likely mean?

choices.text: The airplane is declaring an emergency to nearby traffic
The airplane is operating under a special waiver for low flight
Nothing unusual; these lights are used day and night

explanation.correct: Nothing unusual; these lights are used day and night.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-3-24 says aircraft equipped with an anti-collision light system are required to operate it during all types of operations, day and night, unless the pilot determines it would be a hazard in adverse weather. A flashing beacon in daylight is normal and is not an emergency signal or a sign of a waiver. It can help the remote pilot spot the airplane.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Manned aircraft run anti-collision lights day and night.

stem: A wildlife researcher wants to fly at night without any anti-collision light so the light will not disturb animals. What does Part 107 allow?

choices.text: Only with a certificate of waiver from the FAA
Never; the night lighting requirement cannot be waived
Any time the remote PIC judges it safer to turn the light off

explanation.correct: Only with a certificate of waiver from the FAA.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.29(a)(2) requires anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles at night. The remote PIC may reduce its intensity but may not extinguish it. Section 107.205(b) lists 107.29(a)(2) and (b) among the regulations that can be waived, and AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.7.2.3, describes requesting a waiver of the lighting requirement. So flying without the light is possible only under a waiver, not by the pilot's own judgment.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Night with no anti-collision light requires a waiver. Dimming is allowed; turning it off is not.

stem: While monitoring a radio near an airport, a remote pilot hears an airplane talking to 'Center.' What is an Air Route Traffic Control Center?

choices.text: An ATC facility serving IFR traffic en route
The control tower that runs the airport's traffic pattern
A flight service station that gives weather briefings

explanation.correct: An ATC facility serving IFR traffic en route.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-1 says Air Route Traffic Control Centers are established primarily to provide air traffic service to aircraft operating on IFR flight plans within controlled airspace, principally during the en route phase of flight. AIM 4-1-2 says control towers provide for the flow of traffic on and in the vicinity of an airport. Flight service stations provide briefings and other services but are not Centers.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Center handles en route IFR traffic. The tower handles the airport.

stem: On a sectional chart, a job site lies inside the innermost Class B sector, which is labeled 100 over SFC. The drone will fly at 100 feet AGL. Is ATC authorization required?

choices.text: No; Class B begins well above 400 feet AGL everywhere
Yes; that sector of Class B starts at the surface
Yes, but only because the drone is above 50 feet AGL

explanation.correct: Yes; that sector of Class B starts at the surface.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says Class B ceiling and floor altitudes are shown in solid blue figures with the last two zeros omitted, so 100 over SFC means the sector runs from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL. 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization to operate in Class B airspace. Some outer Class B sectors begin well above the ground, but this one begins at the surface, so even 100 feet AGL is inside it. There is no 50-foot threshold; any altitude in a surface-based Class B sector needs authorization.
explanation.keyTakeaway: SFC as the floor means Class B starts at the ground. Any altitude there needs authorization.

stem: A job site is inside the solid magenta 30-nautical-mile Mode C ring around a Class B primary airport, but outside every blue Class B boundary. The airspace at the surface there is Class G. Is ATC authorization required for a flight at 300 feet AGL?

choices.text: No; the Mode C ring is an equipment area, not Class B
Yes; everything inside the Mode C ring is Class B airspace
No, but the drone needs a Mode C transponder inside the ring

explanation.correct: No; the Mode C ring is an equipment area, not Class B.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says the Mode C required airspace within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport is depicted with a solid magenta line, separate from the solid blue Class B boundaries. It sets an equipment requirement for manned aircraft (14 CFR 91.215), not a class of airspace. 14 CFR 107.41 requires authorization only in Class B, C, or D airspace or a Class E surface area, so a flight in Class G inside the ring needs none. Part 107 prohibits operating with a transponder on unless the FAA authorizes it (107.52), and 14 CFR 91.1(f) says Part 91, including 91.215, generally does not apply to Part 107 aircraft.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The 30 NM Mode C ring is an equipment area, not Class B. Check the actual airspace class.

stem: A Class B sector on a sectional chart is labeled 80 over 25. What does the label mean?

choices.text: Class B from 2,500 feet MSL up to 8,000 feet MSL
Class B from 2,500 feet AGL up to 8,000 feet AGL
Class B from 250 feet MSL up to 800 feet MSL

explanation.correct: Class B from 2,500 feet MSL up to 8,000 feet MSL.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says Class B ceiling and floor altitudes are MSL values shown in solid blue figures with the last two zeros omitted. 80 over 25 means a ceiling of 8,000 feet MSL and a floor of 2,500 feet MSL. The numbers are MSL, not AGL, and the omitted digits are two zeros, so 25 is 2,500, not 250.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class B labels: ceiling over floor, MSL, add two zeros.

stem: A Class B shelf over a job site has a floor of 1,500 feet MSL. The ground at the site is 1,300 feet MSL, and the drone will fly at 300 feet AGL. Is the drone in Class B airspace?

choices.text: Yes, because every Class B shelf begins at the surface
No; the shelf floor is 1,500 feet AGL, far above the drone
Yes; 300 feet AGL is 1,600 feet MSL, above the shelf's floor

explanation.correct: Yes; 300 feet AGL is 1,600 feet MSL, above the shelf's floor.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says Class B floor altitudes are charted in MSL. With the ground at 1,300 feet MSL, a drone at 300 feet AGL is at 1,600 feet MSL, which is above the 1,500-foot MSL floor, so it is inside Class B and needs prior ATC authorization under 14 CFR 107.41. Reading the floor as AGL, or assuming a minimum height for shelves, gives the wrong answer on high ground. Class B shelves have floors above the surface; this one starts at 1,500 feet MSL, which the drone exceeds only because the ground is high.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Convert AGL to MSL before comparing with a Class B floor, especially on high ground.

stem: On a sectional chart, a Class C shelf is labeled T over 12. What does the T mean?

choices.text: Class C applies only while the control tower is operating
The shelf is a temporary flight restriction area
Class C goes up to, but not into, the overlying Class B

explanation.correct: Class C goes up to, but not into, the overlying Class B.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says a Class C ceiling value of 'T' indicates the ceiling is to, but not including, the floor of the overlying Class B airspace. The floor here is 1,200 feet MSL. Part-time Class C is shown with a separate note, and the T has nothing to do with TFRs.
explanation.keyTakeaway: T in a Class C label: up to the overlying Class B floor.

stem: A job site is 3 nautical miles from a Class C primary airport, inside the inner magenta circle labeled 40 over SFC. Is authorization required for a flight at 100 feet AGL?

choices.text: Yes; that part of Class C extends from the surface
Yes, but only for flights above 200 feet AGL
No; Class C requires only two-way radio contact for drones

explanation.correct: Yes; that part of Class C extends from the surface.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-4 says Class C usually consists of a 5 NM radius core surface area from the surface up to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation, and the FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide shows SFC as the floor in the magenta label. A site 3 NM from the airport inside that core is in Class C at any altitude, so 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization. The 1,200-foot floor applies to the outer shelf. Two-way radio contact is the manned-aircraft entry requirement. No altitude exempts a flight inside the Class C core.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class C core: surface up. Prior authorization, not radio contact.

stem: A job site is beyond the outer magenta circle of a Class C area, in Class G airspace at the surface. A magenta box nearby lists the approach control frequency for arriving VFR aircraft. Is ATC authorization required for a drone at 300 feet AGL?

choices.text: No, but only after calling the listed frequency first
Yes; the frequency box means radio contact is required here
No; the site is outside the Class C airspace boundary

explanation.correct: No; the site is outside the Class C airspace boundary.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says Class C is shown in solid magenta with its floor and ceiling, and separate magenta notes give approach control frequencies that arriving VFR aircraft use to establish radio contact before entering Class C. Those notes do not extend Class C. Outside the outer circle, the site is not in Class C, so 14 CFR 107.41 does not require authorization in the Class G airspace there. Part 107 never requires the remote pilot to call approach control; the site is simply outside Class C.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Frequency boxes guide manned arrivals. They do not expand Class C.

stem: The AIM describes a Class C 'outer area.' What is it?

choices.text: A charted shelf that requires ATC authorization to enter
An uncharted area, normally 20 NM out, where ATC offers services
A ring where drones need radio contact with approach control

explanation.correct: An uncharted area, normally 20 NM out, where ATC offers services.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-4 says Class C airspace areas have a procedural Outer Area, normally 20 NM from the primary Class C airport, in which ATC provides services, and that this outer area is not charted. It excludes the Class C airspace itself, so it is not part of Class C and needs no authorization under 14 CFR 107.41. Part 107 never requires a drone to be in radio contact with ATC.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The Class C outer area is not Class C. It is an uncharted service area for manned traffic.

stem: A job site lies inside the Class C surface area of a primary airport, right next to a small non-towered satellite airport. The pilot reasons that a non-towered airport needs no authorization. Is that correct?

choices.text: No; satellite airports always have their own Class D
Yes; satellite airports are excluded from Class C
No; the site is still inside Class C airspace

explanation.correct: No; the site is still inside Class C airspace.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-4 describes satellite airports, with or without an operating control tower, located within Class C airspace, and sets communication rules for aircraft departing them. Being near a non-towered satellite airport does not remove the airspace around it from Class C. 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization to operate in Class C airspace, so the pilot needs authorization here. The satellite airport here has no Class D of its own; the airspace around it is the primary airport's Class C.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A satellite airport inside Class C is still in Class C. The airspace class decides, not the tower.

stem: Inside a Class D airport's dashed blue boundary, a box shows -30. What does the minus sign mean?

choices.text: Class D begins 3,000 feet below the overlying Class B airspace
Class D runs from 3,000 feet MSL down to the surface at night only
Class D runs from the surface up to, but not including, 3,000 feet MSL

explanation.correct: Class D runs from the surface up to, but not including, 3,000 feet MSL.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says a minus in front of a Class D ceiling figure indicates 'from surface to, but not including' that altitude. -30 therefore means from the surface up to, but not including, 3,000 feet MSL. It does not refer to Class B airspace, and it has nothing to do with time of day.
explanation.keyTakeaway: A minus before a Class D ceiling means up to, but not including, that MSL altitude.

stem: An airport's part-time Class D airspace has a Class E arrival extension shown by a dashed magenta line. The Chart Supplement says the Class D becomes Class G when the tower closes. After hours, a remote pilot flies at 200 feet AGL inside the extension. Is ATC authorization required?

choices.text: No; the extension becomes Class G along with it
Yes; arrival extensions stay Class E at all times
No, but only if the drone stays below 100 feet AGL

explanation.correct: No; the extension becomes Class G along with it.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-5 says surface area arrival extensions are effective during the published times of the surface area: for part-time Class D surface areas that revert to Class E, the arrival extensions remain in effect as Class E airspace, but for part-time Class D surface areas that change to Class G, the arrival extensions become Class G at the same time. Here the Class D becomes Class G, so the extension does too, and 14 CFR 107.41 requires no authorization. No altitude threshold such as 100 feet is involved.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Arrival extensions follow their surface area: Class G after hours if the surface area becomes Class G.

stem: A remote pilot holds a LAANC authorization for a flight inside Class D airspace. Must the pilot also establish two-way radio contact with the tower before launching?

choices.text: Yes; every aircraft in Class D must be in radio contact with the tower
No; Part 107 requires prior authorization, not radio contact
No, but the drone must carry an aviation radio

explanation.correct: No; Part 107 requires prior authorization, not radio contact.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior authorization from ATC to operate in Class D airspace, and AIM 11-1-2 says LAANC is one way Part 107 operators request it. The two-way radio requirement in AIM 4-3-2 applies to manned aircraft operating in the surface area of a towered airport. Part 107 does not require a radio, and LAANC authorization does not depend on a radio call. Part 107 does not require the drone or the pilot to carry an aviation radio.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class D for drones: get the authorization. Radio contact is the manned-aircraft rule.

stem: A job site is a quarter mile outside a Class D airport's dashed blue boundary, in Class G airspace at the surface. Is ATC authorization required for a flight at 200 feet AGL?

choices.text: Yes; any flight within 1 mile of Class D needs authorization
No; authorization applies only inside the Class D boundary
No, but only because the drone stays below 400 feet AGL

explanation.correct: No; authorization applies only inside the Class D boundary.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide identifies Class D with a dashed blue line. 14 CFR 107.41 requires authorization only within Class D airspace (and Class B, C, and Class E surface areas). A site outside the dashed blue line in Class G needs no authorization, although the pilot must still avoid interfering with airport traffic under 107.43. Part 107 has no 1-mile buffer. The 400-foot limit does not decide this; the site is outside the Class D boundary.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The dashed blue line is the Class D boundary. Outside it, check what airspace you are actually in.

stem: A job site lies under a band of blue vignette (fading blue shading) on a sectional chart, and the drone will fly at 400 feet AGL. What does this tell the remote pilot?

choices.text: Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL, so 400 feet AGL is Class G
Class E begins at the surface there, so authorization is required
The area is Class B airspace, so authorization is required

explanation.correct: Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL, so 400 feet AGL is Class G.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says controlled airspace floors of 700 feet AGL are shown by magenta vignette, and floors other than 700 feet that abut Class G are shown by blue vignette; AIM 3-2-6 says Class E transition areas begin at either 700 feet AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 feet AGL (blue vignette). Below that floor is Class G, which needs no authorization under 14 CFR 107.41. A Class E surface area is a dashed magenta line, and Class B is solid blue lines.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Magenta vignette: Class E at 700 AGL. Blue vignette: Class E at 1,200 AGL. Below either: Class G.

stem: A drone flies at 300 feet AGL beneath a Federal (Victor) airway shown on the sectional chart, far from any airport. What class of airspace is the drone in?

choices.text: Class G; the airway's Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL
Class E, because airways extend down to the surface
Class B, because airways connect major airports

explanation.correct: Class G; the airway's Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-6 says Federal airways and low-altitude RNAV routes are Class E airspace that, unless otherwise specified, extends upward from 1,200 feet AGL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL. A drone at 300 feet AGL below an airway is in the Class G airspace beneath it, with no authorization required under 14 CFR 107.41. Airways do not reach the surface, and they are not Class B.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Victor airways are Class E from 1,200 feet AGL. Drones below them are usually in Class G.

stem: A small airport with no control tower is surrounded by a dashed magenta line on the sectional chart. A remote pilot assumes that with no tower, no authorization is needed. Is that correct?

choices.text: Yes; airports without a tower never require an authorization
No; dashed magenta marks a Class E surface area needing authorization
No; a dashed magenta line marks Class B airspace

explanation.correct: No; dashed magenta marks a Class E surface area needing authorization.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says Class E surface airspace is shown with a dashed magenta line, and AIM 3-2-6 describes Class E surface areas designated for airports where a control tower is not in operation. 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior ATC authorization within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport. Having no tower does not remove that requirement. Class B is shown with solid blue lines, not dashed magenta.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Dashed magenta around an airport means authorization, tower or no tower.

stem: The Chart Supplement says an airport's Class E surface area is in effect only part-time and is 'other times Class G.' A remote pilot flies at 200 feet AGL inside the dashed magenta line during the other times. Is authorization required?

choices.text: Yes; the dashed magenta line always requires authorization
No; during those other times the area is Class G
No; Class E surface areas never need authorization

explanation.correct: No; during those other times the area is Class G.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says a Class E surface area operating less than continuously is marked with a note on the chart, and AIM 3-2-6 says pilots should refer to the airport page in the Chart Supplement for surface area status information. During 'other times Class G,' 14 CFR 107.41 requires no authorization. The 700- and 1,200-foot transition areas, by contrast, remain in effect continuously (AIM 3-2-6). While in effect, a Class E surface area does need authorization under 107.41; it is the part-time Class G status that removes the need.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part-time surface areas: the Chart Supplement says what applies after hours.

stem: In Class G airspace, manned VFR pilots may fly with less visibility and closer to clouds at low altitudes than in controlled airspace. Does that relax the Part 107 weather minimums?

choices.text: Yes; drones in Class G may use the manned Class G minimums
No; drones in Class G need 5 statute miles
No; Part 107's visibility and cloud minimums apply in every class

explanation.correct: No; Part 107's visibility and cloud minimums apply in every class.
explanation.reason: Manned VFR weather minimums are set by 14 CFR 91.155 and vary by airspace class (AIM 3-3-2). Part 107 sets its own minimums in 14 CFR 107.51(c) and (d): 3 statute miles of flight visibility from the control station, and at least 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. Those apply in all airspace, including Class G. Part 107 sets 3 statute miles in every class, not 5.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Part 107 weather minimums are the same in every airspace class, including Class G.

stem: How does the AIM define Class G airspace?

choices.text: Airspace below 400 feet AGL reserved for unmanned aircraft
Airspace within 5 miles of an airport with no control tower
Airspace not designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E

explanation.correct: Airspace not designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-3-1 says Class G (uncontrolled) airspace is that portion of airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D, or E. It is not reserved for drones, and it is not defined by distance from airports. Manned aircraft fly in Class G too.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Class G is whatever is left over after Classes A through E.

stem: On a sectional chart, an airport symbol is drawn in magenta, and there are no dashed lines or vignette shading around it. What do the color and the missing markings tell the remote pilot?

choices.text: An operating control tower, and Class D around it
No control tower, but Class E down to the surface
No control tower, and Class G at the surface around it

explanation.correct: No control tower, and Class G at the surface around it.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says airports with control towers are shown in blue and all other airports in magenta. It shows Class D with a dashed blue line, Class E surface areas with a dashed magenta line, and 700-foot Class E floors with magenta vignette, and it says Class E exists at 1,200 feet AGL unless designated otherwise. With none of those markings, the airspace at the surface is Class G, so 14 CFR 107.41 requires no authorization, though 107.43 still prohibits interfering with the airport's traffic.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Magenta airport = no tower. No dashed lines or vignette = Class G at the surface.

stem: A remote pilot plans a flight inside a military operations area and wants to know whether it is active. According to the AIM, how can the pilot find out?

choices.text: Look for flashing lights on the ground along the area's boundary
Assume it is inactive unless a NOTAM says otherwise
Contact a flight service station within 100 miles of the area

explanation.correct: Contact a flight service station within 100 miles of the area.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-4-5 says the active or inactive status of an MOA may change frequently, and pilots should contact any flight service station within 100 miles of the area for accurate real-time information on hours of operation. VFR pilots should use extreme caution in an active MOA. There are no boundary lights, and because MOA status changes often, the AIM sends pilots to flight service for real-time status rather than leaving them to assume.
explanation.keyTakeaway: MOA status changes often. Call flight service for current information.

stem: Why do restricted areas require permission from the using or controlling agency before a drone may enter?

choices.text: They may contain unusual, often invisible hazards such as artillery fire or missiles
They are reserved for airline arrivals and departures
They contain heavy training traffic, with pilots equally responsible for avoidance

explanation.correct: They may contain unusual, often invisible hazards such as artillery fire or missiles.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-4-3 says restricted areas denote unusual, often invisible hazards to aircraft such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles, and that entering without authorization from the using or controlling agency may be extremely hazardous. 14 CFR 107.45 requires that permission. Heavy training traffic with shared responsibility for avoidance describes an alert area (AIM 3-4-6).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Restricted areas can hold invisible hazards. Get permission first.

stem: According to the AIM, how are hazardous activities in a controlled firing area kept clear of nonparticipating aircraft?

choices.text: Nonparticipating aircraft must get permission to enter
The activity stops when an aircraft might be approaching
ATC closes the airspace each time it becomes active

explanation.correct: The activity stops when an aircraft might be approaching.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-4-7 says the distinguishing feature of a controlled firing area is that its activities are suspended immediately when spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout positions indicate an aircraft might be approaching, and that CFAs are not charted because they do not cause a nonparticipating aircraft to change its flight path. CFAs are nonregulatory special use airspace (AIM 3-4-1), so no permission is required, and the airspace is not closed to other aircraft.
explanation.keyTakeaway: CFA activities halt when aircraft approach. That is why CFAs are not charted.

stem: A sectional chart shows a parachute jumping symbol near a job site. Where can the remote pilot find details on the jump area?

choices.text: The Chart Supplement's jump tables, plus NOTAMs
In the METAR and TAF for the nearest airport
Nowhere; parachute jumping is not regulated or published

explanation.correct: The Chart Supplement's jump tables, plus NOTAMs.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-5-4 says procedures for parachute jump areas are in 14 CFR Part 105 and tabulations of parachute jump areas in the U.S. are contained in the Chart Supplement. The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says pilots are expected to check NOTAMs for miscellaneous activity areas shown on the chart. A METAR does not report jump activity.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Parachute jump areas: check the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs, and expect jumpers.

stem: A remote pilot checks a current sectional chart for temporary flight restrictions near the job site and finds none. Is the site free of TFRs?

choices.text: Yes; every TFR in effect is printed on the current sectional
Not necessarily; only national security TFRs are charted
Not necessarily; TFRs appear only on terminal area charts

explanation.correct: Not necessarily; only national security TFRs are charted.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says a TFR is a type of NOTAM and that only TFRs relating to national security are charted. Other TFRs, such as those for disasters, VIP visits, or sporting events, appear only by NOTAM. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10.3, says the remote PIC must check NOTAMs before each flight. TFRs apply to drones at any altitude within their limits. TFRs are not charted on terminal area charts either; apart from national security TFRs, they are published only by NOTAM.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Most TFRs are not on the chart. NOTAMs are the source.

stem: What service does an airport control tower provide, according to the AIM?

choices.text: Preflight weather briefings and NOTAMs for pilots
A safe, orderly flow of traffic on and near the airport
En route separation for IFR traffic between airports

explanation.correct: A safe, orderly flow of traffic on and near the airport.
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-2 says towers have been established to provide for a safe, orderly, and expeditious flow of traffic on and in the vicinity of an airport. AIM 4-1-3 says flight service stations provide pilot briefings and process NOTAMs, and AIM 4-1-1 says Air Route Traffic Control Centers serve IFR traffic, mainly en route.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Tower: the airport. Center: en route IFR. Flight service: briefings and NOTAMs.

stem: A remote pilot wants a weather briefing and a check of NOTAMs before a job. Which FAA facility provides these services?

choices.text: The nearest airport control tower
A flight service station (FSS)
An Air Route Traffic Control Center

explanation.correct: A flight service station (FSS).
explanation.reason: AIM 4-1-3 says flight service stations are air traffic facilities that provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route flight advisories, search and rescue services, and assistance to aircraft in emergencies, and that they process NOTAMs and broadcast weather and aeronautical information. Towers manage traffic on and near an airport (AIM 4-1-2), and Centers serve IFR traffic en route (AIM 4-1-1).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Briefings and NOTAMs come from flight service.

stem: According to the AIM, what is 'controlled airspace'?

choices.text: Airspace where every aircraft must be in radio contact with ATC
Airspace where ATC serves aircraft according to its class
Any airspace within 5 statute miles of an airport

explanation.correct: Airspace where ATC serves aircraft according to its class.
explanation.reason: AIM 3-2-1 says controlled airspace is a generic term covering Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace, with defined dimensions within which ATC service is provided to IFR flights and to VFR flights in accordance with the airspace classification. Radio requirements for manned aircraft vary by class, and controlled airspace is not defined by distance from an airport. For drones, 14 CFR 107.41 requires authorization in Classes B, C, D, and Class E surface areas.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Controlled airspace = Classes A through E, where ATC provides service by class.

stem: From the control station, flight visibility is 4 statute miles. A bank of fog lies on the ground about 1,000 feet to one side of the planned flight path, and other clouds are well above. May the drone fly that path as planned?

choices.text: Yes; 4 miles of visibility meets the 3-mile minimum
No; any fog in the area grounds all drone flights
No; fog is cloud, so the drone must stay 2,000 feet from it

explanation.correct: No; fog is cloud, so the drone must stay 2,000 feet from it.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.51(c) is met, because flight visibility from the control station is at least 3 statute miles. But 107.51(d) also requires the drone to stay at least 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds, and the PHAK (FAA-H-8083-25C) says fog is a cloud that is on the surface. A path 1,000 feet from the fog bank breaks the 2,000-foot horizontal clearance. Moving the path at least 2,000 feet from the fog would make the flight legal, so fog nearby does not ground every flight.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Fog is cloud on the ground. Keep 2,000 feet horizontally from it.

stem: Visibility at a Class D airport is 2 statute miles, and the tower is issuing special VFR clearances to airplanes. A remote pilot asks the tower for one so the drone can fly. Can the tower grant it?

choices.text: No; special VFR is a Part 91 rule that does not apply to drones
Yes; the tower can clear a drone for special VFR the same way
No; special VFR would also require a transponder on the drone

explanation.correct: No; special VFR is a Part 91 rule that does not apply to drones.
explanation.reason: Special VFR is in 14 CFR 91.157, and 91.1(f) says Part 91 does not apply to aircraft governed by Part 107 except for a short list of sections that does not include 91.157. Part 107 requires at least 3 statute miles of flight visibility from the control station (107.51(c)); lower visibility is possible only under a certificate of waiver (107.205 lists 107.51). A transponder has nothing to do with it, and 107.52 prohibits operating a small UAS with a transponder on unless authorized.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Drones get no special VFR. Below 3 SM, only a waiver helps.

stem: The UAS Facility Map value over a job site in Class D airspace is 100 feet. The pilot needs 250 feet AGL. What does the AIM say?

choices.text: Fly to 250 feet, because the map values are only suggestions
Nothing can be done; 100 feet is the absolute limit at that site
Request further coordination; 100 feet is the automatic approval limit

explanation.correct: Request further coordination; 100 feet is the automatic approval limit.
explanation.reason: AIM 11-1-2 says operations in controlled airspace can be readily approved up to the altitude values on the UAS Facility Map, which are the maximum altitudes that can be approved without further coordination with the ATC facility. Part 107 operators may request further coordination for an authorization above those values, up to 400 feet AGL. Flying above an authorization's altitude is flying without authorization, and the map value is not an absolute ceiling.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Facility map value = automatic approval limit. Above it, ask for further coordination.

stem: A LAANC authorization covers a flight from 2:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. The job runs late. At 3:10 p.m., may the pilot keep flying in the controlled airspace?

choices.text: No; the authorization covers only its approved time and limits
Yes; an authorization stays valid for the rest of the day
No, unless the pilot radios the tower first

explanation.correct: No; the authorization covers only its approved time and limits.
explanation.reason: 14 CFR 107.41 requires prior authorization from ATC to operate in controlled airspace. AC 107-2A, paragraph 5.10, says ATC authorizations may depend on operational parameters and that the FAA may approve or deny operations based on traffic density, controller workload, and other factors. An authorization approved for 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. does not cover 3:10 p.m., so continuing is operating without prior authorization; the pilot must land and obtain a new or extended authorization. An authorization does not last for the rest of the day, and a radio call does not extend it: Part 107 requires prior authorization (through LAANC or DroneZone, AIM 11-1-2), not radio contact.
explanation.keyTakeaway: An authorization's time window is a limit, just like its altitude.

stem: An airport data block on the sectional chart shows RP 23. A remote pilot is working on the side of the field where right traffic for runway 23 would fly. What does RP 23 tell the pilot?

choices.text: Runway 23 is restricted to private aircraft
Runway 23 is closed, so no traffic will use it
Runway 23 uses a right-hand traffic pattern

explanation.correct: Runway 23 uses a right-hand traffic pattern.
explanation.reason: The FAA Aeronautical Chart Users' Guide says right traffic information is shown with the abbreviation RP for right pattern followed by the runway number, and an asterisk (*RP) points to the Chart Supplement for restrictions.
